method: Water is quoted by volume against the dry rice, so the ratio is cups of water per cup of dry rice: the defaults are 1.75 for long-grain and medium-grain white rice, 1.5 for jasmine and basmati, 1.15 for short-grain sushi rice, 2.25 for brown rice, 3 for wild rice and 4.5 for arborio, and the field can be overridden to match a packet or a measured batch. A cup is 236.5882365 ml and the water in millilitres is the rice volume in cups multiplied by the ratio and by that figure. A gram amount is first turned into cups with the type's bulk density (185 g for long-grain, 180 g for jasmine and basmati, 190 g for medium-grain and brown, 200 g for short-grain and arborio, 160 g for wild rice), because the ratio applies to volume rather than mass. A serving is taken as half a cup of cooked rice, and a serving request is converted back into dry rice with the type's cooked expansion (3 cups cooked per cup dry for most white and brown rice, 2.7 for short-grain, 3.5 for wild), so the cooked volume and serving count are estimates of typical absorption rather than a measurement of the pan. The pot figure is simply the dry rice plus the water. Amounts are refused outside 0.05 to 40 cups, 10 to 6400 grams or 1 to 80 half-cup servings, and ratios outside 0.5 to 8; decimal commas are accepted. The page does not model soaking, evaporation, altitude, stirring or absorption differences between crops, and it makes no food-safety claim about cooking, cooling or storing rice. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cooked rice: rice is generally cooked by absorption with roughly two parts water to one part rice by volume, and one cup of dry white rice yields about three cups cooked, though the exact figures depend on the variety.
Wikipedia, Brown rice: brown rice keeps its bran and germ, so it needs more water and a longer cooking time than white rice.
Wikipedia, Wild rice: wild rice is the grain of a North American water grass rather than a true rice, and the grains split open as they cook.
Wikipedia, Arborio rice: arborio is a short-grain Italian rice used for risotto, cooked by adding hot stock a ladle at a time rather than all at once.
